For measurable real endpoints $\ell\le u$ $Q$-almost everywhere, the bracket $[\ell,u]$ is the set of measurable functions $f$ satisfying $\ell\le f\le u$ $Q$-almost everywhere. Its $L^r(Q)$ width is $\|u-\ell\|_{Q,r}$. Centers of metric covers are in $\mathcal F$; bracket endpoints need not be.

Put $q(t):=P_g(X_{g1}\ge t)$. For $s<t$, the indicators are nested and $P_g|f_s-f_t|=P_g(s\le X_{g1}<t)=q(s)-q(t)$. The function $q$ is nonincreasing with range in $[0,1]$. Let $\Omega$ be a nonempty finite set. Its **uniform probability space** assigns every $\omega\in\Omega$ the weight $1/|\Omega|$. Thus every event $A\subseteq\Omega$ has
$$\mathbb P(A)=\frac{|A|}{|\Omega|}.$$
Nonemptiness is required so that the denominator is positive.

For an event $A$ in a finite probability space, its **indicator random variable** is
$$\mathbf 1_A(\omega):=\begin{cases}1,&\omega\in A,\\0,&\omega\notin A.\end{cases}$$

For a finite family of real random variables $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ on one finite probability space and real scalars $(a_i)_{i\in I}$,
$$\mathbb E\!\left[\sum_{i\in I}a_iX_i\right]=\sum_{i\in I}a_i\mathbb E[X_i].$$
No independence hypothesis is required. For $I=\varnothing$, both sides are $0$.

For every event $A$, $\mathbb E[\mathbf1_A]=\mathbb P(A)$. For every finite family $(A_i)_{i\in I}$,
$$\prod_{i\in I}\mathbf1_{A_i}=\mathbf1_{\cap_{i\in I}A_i},$$
and $\sum_{i\in I}\mathbf1_{A_i}(\omega)$ is the number of events $A_i$ that contain $\omega$. The empty product is $1$ and the empty sum is $0$.

For real random variables $X$ and $Y$ on one finite probability space, define
$$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2],\qquad \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$
The **standard deviation** of $X$ is $\sigma_X:=\operatorname{Var}(X)^{1/2}$, using the unique nonnegative square root supplied by [[thm-of-square-roots]]. Variance is nonnegative because its defining random variable is pointwise nonnegative and expectation is a sum with nonnegative weights.

For finite real random variables $X,Y$,
$$\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb E[X^2]-\mathbb E[X]^2,$$
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathbb E[XY]-\mathbb E[X]\mathbb E[Y].$$
Variance is nonnegative, and every constant random variable has variance zero. Zero variance forces equality to the mean on every positive-weight outcome, but not necessarily on zero-weight outcomes.

Fix a follow-up horizon $\tau>0$ and a finite set of subjects
$\mathcal I=\{1,\ldots,n\}$. A right-censored record for subject $i$ is a
pair $(U_i,\delta_i)\in[0,\tau]\times\{0,1\}$, where
$U_i=\min(T_i,C_i)$ is the observed time and
$\delta_i=1\{T_i\le C_i\}$ records an event, including an event-censoring tie;
$\delta_i=0$ records right censoring. A two-group assignment is a map
$z:\mathcal I\to\{0,1\}$. These conventions are the right-censoring
observation scheme; the score below uses the observed record and does not
infer event or censoring laws from it.

Let $t_1<\cdots<t_K$ be the distinct observed failure times in $[0,\tau]$.
For $g\in\{0,1\}$ define the risk count and event count at $t_j$ by
$$Y_{gj}(z):=\#\{i:z_i=g,\ U_i\ge t_j\},\qquad d_{gj}(z):=\#\{i:z_i=g,\ U_i=t_j,\ \delta_i=1\}.$$
Write $Y_j=Y_{0j}+Y_{1j}$, $d_j=d_{0j}+d_{1j}>0$, and
$O_j=d_{1j}$. Since $t_j$ is an observed failure time,
$1\le d_j\le Y_j$. The expected group-1 count under the conditional
hypergeometric model is
$$E_j:=d_j\frac{Y_{1j}}{Y_j}.$$
Under that model the $d_j$ failing subjects are a uniform $d_j$-subset of the
$Y_j$ subjects at risk, conditional on the risk-set and event-count margins.
The corresponding conditional variance is
$$V_j:= \begin{cases} \displaystyle\frac{Y_{1j}Y_{0j}d_j(Y_j-d_j)} {Y_j^2(Y_j-1)},&Y_j>1,\\[6pt] 0,&Y_j=1. \end{cases}$$
If the study has no observed failures, all sums below are empty and equal zero.
The conditional hypergeometric model is an explicit finite risk-set
assumption; equality of survival laws with arbitrary censoring or subject
heterogeneity does not by itself assert this conditional allocation law.
The uniform law on the finite set of $d_j$-subsets is the uniform finite
probability space of [[def-uniform-finite-probability-space]].

A **weight rule** assigns a real value $w_j$ using only the predeclared time
and information available strictly before the failures at $t_j$; deterministic
bounded time weights are a special case. If
$\sup_j|w_j|<\infty$, define the weighted logrank score and its conditional
variance estimate by
$$U_w(z;U,\delta):=\sum_{j=1}^K w_j(O_j-E_j),\qquad \widehat V_w(z;U,\delta):=\sum_{j=1}^K w_j^2V_j.$$
When $\widehat V_w>0$, set
$Z_w:=U_w/\sqrt{\widehat V_w}$. If $\widehat V_w=0$, this standardized
statistic is left undefined; the unstandardized score remains defined. The
normal calibration is only an approximation until the separate terminal
limit hypotheses are verified. It is not the finite-sample Fisher
randomization p-value.

derivations.claim: If $Y=0$, then $d=0$, $O=0$, and both stated moments are zero. Suppose $Y\ge1$. For each of the $Y_1$ group-1 subjects let $I_a$ indicate that subject $a$ is in the failing subset. Under [A1], when $d\ge1$, $P(I_a=1)=\binom{Y-1}{d-1}/\binom{Y}{d}=d/Y$; for $d=0$, both sides are zero. Since $O=\sum_{a=1}^{Y_1}I_a$, [F3] and [F4] give $\mathbb E O=Y_1d/Y$.
If $Y=1$, then $d\in\{0,1\}$ and the failing subset is deterministic: $O=dY_1$. Its expectation is $dY_1/Y$ and its variance is zero, as stipulated.

Suppose $Y>1$. For distinct group-1 subjects $a,b$, if $d\ge2$ the same subset count gives $P(I_a=I_b=1)=\binom{Y-2}{d-2}/\binom{Y}{d}=d(d-1)/(Y(Y-1))$; for $d=0$ or $d=1$ the probability and the displayed ratio are both zero. In the sequential model, step 1.1 and the $Y_j=0$ convention give $\mathbb E[O_j-E_j\mid\mathcal H_{j-1}]=0$, and step 2.1 gives conditional variance $V_j$. If $k<j$, the filtration property and the revelation convention make $D_k$ $\mathcal H_{j-1}$-measurable, so $\mathbb E[D_kD_j]=\mathbb E[D_k\,\mathbb E(D_j\mid\mathcal H_{j-1})]=0$. Let $N\ge1$, and let $\mathcal I=\{1,\ldots,N\}$ index the fixed
experimental units at the actual treatment-assignment level. Let
$\mathcal Z$ be a nonempty finite set of allowed assignments. If treatment
is assigned to clusters, each cluster is one indexed unit; no separate
probability-sampling unit is present. The index $i$ identifies that unit,
and no visit or repeated-measurement index is modeled here.

A known assignment law is a function $p:\mathcal Z\to[0,1]$ satisfying
$\sum_{z\in\mathcal Z}p(z)=1$, so $(\mathcal Z,p)$ is a finite probability
space ([[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]); assignments of probability
zero may remain in $\mathcal Z$. A **potential-outcome schedule** is a function
$\theta:\mathcal I\times\mathcal Z\to\mathbb R$, with
$Y_i(z):=\theta(i,z)$. The schedule and the units are fixed; the assignment
$Z$ is the only randomness supplied by the design, and the observed response
vector is $Y_\theta(Z)=(Y_i(Z))_{i\in\mathcal I}$. The schedule is defined
for every allowed assignment, including zero-probability assignments, and
may depend on the full assignment vector, so no no-interference assumption is
implicit. The scientific statistical model contract
[[def-scientific-statistical-model-contract]] requires the observation space,
units, quantity status, observation mechanism, support, conditioning
convention, and adequacy assumptions to be recorded; this model specifies
those fields as follows.

To express this as a statistical experiment, take the data space
$\mathcal X=\mathcal Z\times\mathbb R^{\mathcal I}$ with its full power-set
sigma-algebra, which is a sigma-algebra by [[def-sigma-algebra]] and makes
$\mathcal X$ a measurable space ([[def-measurable-space]]), and parameter
set $\Theta=\mathbb R^{\mathcal I\times\mathcal Z}$. For each $\theta\in\Theta$
let $P_\theta$ be the law
([[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]) of the deterministic
observation map $O_\theta(z)=(z,Y_\theta(z))$ from $(\mathcal Z,p)$. The map
is measurable because its domain has the full power set, in the preimage

$$S_\theta:=\{(z,Y_\theta(z)):z\in\mathcal Z,\ p(z)>0\},$$

inferential target is the assignment-invariance hypothesis for these $N$

The status of the quantities is explicit: $\theta$ and all

determines $Y_\theta(z)$. Assignment invariance on this positive-probability

invariance hypothesis on all allowed assignments. Values at assignments

untestable** from this law, since changing them leaves $P_\theta$ unchanged.

empirically true.

A **predeclared ordering score** is a real-valued statistic
$T:\mathcal Z\times\mathbb R^{\mathcal I}\to\mathbb R$
([[def-statistic-and-estimator]]) fixed before the
assignment and outcomes are inspected. Its upper-tail ordering includes ties:

two-sided ordering is explicitly $T(z,y)=|S(z,y)-s_0|$. The center is part

for an arbitrary signed score. A lower-tail ordering is represented by
using $-S$ as the score. A statistic in this setting is a measurable map in
the sense of [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]; the full power-set data

$\delta_i=1\{T_i\le C_i\}$ records an event, including an event-censoring tie;

$z:\mathcal I\to\{0,1\}$. These conventions are the right-censoring
observation scheme; the score below uses the observed record and does not
infer event or censoring laws from it.

Let $t_1<\cdots<t_K$ be the distinct observed failure times in $[0,\tau]$.
For $g\in\{0,1\}$ define the risk count and event count at $t_j$ by
$$Y_{gj}(z):=\#\{i:z_i=g,\ U_i\ge t_j\},\qquad d_{gj}(z):=\#\{i:z_i=g,\ U_i=t_j,\ \delta_i=1\}.$$
Write $Y_j=Y_{0j}+Y_{1j}$, $d_j=d_{0j}+d_{1j}>0$, and
$O_j=d_{1j}$. Since $t_j$ is an observed failure time,
$1\le d_j\le Y_j$. The expected group-1 count under the conditional
hypergeometric model is
$$E_j:=d_j\frac{Y_{1j}}{Y_j}.$$
Under that model the $d_j$ failing subjects are a uniform $d_j$-subset of the
$Y_j$ subjects at risk, conditional on the risk-set and event-count margins.
The corresponding conditional variance is
$$V_j:= \begin{cases} \displaystyle\frac{Y_{1j}Y_{0j}d_j(Y_j-d_j)} {Y_j^2(Y_j-1)},&Y_j>1,\\[6pt] 0,&Y_j=1. \end{cases}$$
If the study has no observed failures, all sums below are empty and equal zero.

assumption; equality of survival laws with arbitrary censoring or subject
heterogeneity does not by itself assert this conditional allocation law.
The uniform law on the finite set of $d_j$-subsets is the uniform finite
probability space of [[def-uniform-finite-probability-space]].

A **weight rule** assigns a real value $w_j$ using only the predeclared time
and information available strictly before the failures at $t_j$; deterministic
bounded time weights are a special case. If
$\sup_j|w_j|<\infty$, define the weighted logrank score and its conditional
variance estimate by
$$U_w(z;U,\delta):=\sum_{j=1}^K w_j(O_j-E_j),\qquad \widehat V_w(z;U,\delta):=\sum_{j=1}^K w_j^2V_j.$$

statistic is left undefined; the unstandardized score remains defined. The
normal calibration is only an approximation until the separate terminal
limit hypotheses are verified. It is not the finite-sample Fisher
randomization p-value.

cause whose failures are conditionally exchangeable. This definition does
not pool different causes or add their variances without a specified
cross-cause covariance model.

be an experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **statistic** with target
measurable space $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ is a measurable map

means that $T^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B$
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). If
$\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal Y$ is an estimand ([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]])
and its target set $\mathcal Y$ is equipped with $\mathcal B$, a statistic
$\widehat\psi$ with this same target space is an **estimator of $\psi$**.
The value $\widehat\psi(x)$ is the estimate at observed data $x$. Giving

does not assert that $\psi$ is measurable as a function of the parameter.

sigma-algebra $2^{\mathcal X}\otimes\mathcal B([0,1])$ and define

$$P_\theta\!\left(p_{\rm rand}(Z,Y_\theta(Z))\le u\right)\le u,$$
whereas the added randomization gives
$$\widetilde P_\theta\!\left(p^+(Z,Y_\theta(Z),U)\le u\right)=u.$$

independent uniform randomizer is used. For a two-sided test, take

uses the actual, possibly unequal assignment probabilities; random
assignment supplies no Gaussian error law, and this theorem makes no
validity claim under the weak zero-average-effect null from
[[def-finite-population-average-treatment-effect-and-weak-null]] unless it
is also Fisher-sharp.

be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **p-value
statistic** is a statistic $p:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$, where $[0,1]$ carries the
trace of the Borel sigma-algebra, meaning

([[def-statistic-and-estimator]],
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]).

$$P_\theta(\{x:p(x)\le u\})\le u\qquad\text{for every }\theta\in\Theta_0\text{ and }u\in[0,1].$$

validity condition is distributional; measurability alone does not imply it.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Fix a finite horizon
$T>0$, a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ and a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ in the all-pairs convention of
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. A **simple
unit-jump counting process** is an adapted, càdlàg (right-continuous with left
limits), nondecreasing, integer-valued process $N$ with $N_0=0$,
$N_T<\infty$ almost surely, and $\Delta N_t\in\{0,1\}$ for every
$0<t\le T$ outside one null event; here $\Delta N_t:=N_t-N_{t-}$.

An **at-risk process** is a predictable process
$Y:[0,T]\times\Omega\to\{0,1\}$, and an **intensity density** is a finite,
nonnegative predictable process $\lambda$. Form the Lebesgue integral
$$A_t:=\int_0^tY_s\lambda_s\,ds,\qquad 0\le t\le T.$$
For this model and every nonnegative predictable process $G$, define the
pathwise energy integral by
$$\int_0^tG_s\,dA_s:=\int_0^tG_sY_s\lambda_s\,ds,\qquad t\le T.$$
The **continuous intensity compensator contract** requires the defining
integral for $A$ to be finite pathwise, and requires $A$ to be continuous,
adapted and predictable with
$A_0=0$, and that $\mathbb E[A_T]<\infty$. Set $M_t:=N_t-A_t$. The model
contract is the additional hypothesis that $M$ is a square-integrable
martingale relative to the stated filtration. Under this contract $A$ is a
continuous predictable compensator of $N$.

The displayed intensity density alone does **not** assert that $N-A$ is a
martingale, that such a process exists for a given $N$, or that the contract
follows from an empirical observation scheme. No general compensator-existence
theorem is included here. The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the
continuous-time martingale and conditional-expectation interfaces; no further
choice is used to state the model contract.

For the compensator contract on $[0,T]$, let $H$ be a predictable real
process with
$$\mathbb E\int_0^T H_s^2\,dA_s<\infty.$$
When the elementary integrals of a sequence of bounded predictable step
processes converging to $H$ in this norm converge in $L^2(P)$, denote the
resulting $L^2(P)$ class at time $t$ by
$$\int_0^t H_s\,dM_s.$$
The definition is conditional on existence of the limit. The L²-extension
theorem below proves existence for every such predictable $H$, independence
from the approximating sequence, the martingale property, and the isometry.
The Axiom of Choice is inherited through the conditional-expectation and
$L^2$-completion interfaces used by that theorem.

Under the finite-horizon contract of
[[def-counting-process-intensity-and-compensator-contract]], the optional
quadratic variation of $M=N-A$ is $[M]_t=N_t$, its continuous predictable
bracket is $\langle M\rangle_t=A_t$, its self-cross predictable bracket is
$\langle M,M\rangle_t=A_t$, and $M_t^2-A_t$ is a martingale on $[0,T]$.

For every predictable $H$ on $[0,T]$ with
$\mathbb E\int_0^T H_s^2\,dA_s<\infty$, the limit in
[[def-l2-counting-process-integral]] exists at each $t\le T$, is independent
of the approximating step sequence, and defines a square-integrable
martingale. It satisfies, for each $t\le T$,
$$\mathbb E\left(\int_0^tH_s\,dM_s\right)^2=\mathbb E\int_0^tH_s^2\,dA_s.$$

For each $g\in\{0,1\}$, let $(U_{gi})_{i\ge1}$ be IID measurable

the two groups is not required. Along a sequence of deterministic positive

Then, for $g=0,1$,
$$\sup_{t\le\tau}\left|\frac{Y_{g,n}(t)}n-y_g(t)\right|\longrightarrow_P0,$$

$$\sup_{0\le t\le\tau}\left|p_n(t)-\bar z(t)\right|\longrightarrow_P0, \qquad \bar z(t):=\frac{y_1(t)}{y(t)}.$$

$\sup_j|w_j|<\infty$, define the weighted logrank score and its conditional

$$U_w(z;U,\delta):=\sum_{j=1}^K w_j(O_j-E_j),\qquad \widehat V_w(z;U,\delta):=\sum_{j=1}^K w_j^2V_j.$$

derivations.claim: Each $Y_{gi}$ is predictable by assumption. Sums of these processes are predictable, and the ratio map $(a,b)\mapsto a/b$ for $b>0$, extended by zero when $b=0$, is Borel; hence $p_n$ is predictable. At an event time $t_j$, the Stieltjes increment of $N_{1,n}$ is $O_j$ and that of $N_n$ is $d_j$. Therefore [F6] gives $ U_{n,w_n}=\int_0^\tau w_n(t)\{dN_{1,n}(t)-p_n(t)dN_n(t)\}. $ Using $dN_{gi}=dM_{gi}+Y_{gi}\lambda(t)\,dt$, the compensator part equals $w_n(t)\{Y_{1,n}(t)-p_n(t)(Y_{0,n}(t)+Y_{1,n}(t))\}\lambda(t)\,dt=0$. Thus, with $M_n=\sum_{g,i}M_{gi}$, $ U_{n,w_n}=\sum_{g,i}\int_0^\tau w_n(t)(g-p_n(t))\,dM_{gi}(t). $

No simultaneous event jumps make $N_n=\sum_{g,i}N_{gi}$ a simple unit-jump counting process. Its compensator is the continuous process $A_n=\sum_{g,i}A_{gi}$, and $M_n=N_n-A_n=\sum_{g,i}M_{gi}$ is a square-integrable martingale by finite summation. Also $A_n(\tau)\le n\Lambda(\tau)$ pathwise. By [F3], $M_n^2-A_n$ is a martingale; [F2]-[F4] apply to the common predictable integrand $H_n=w_n(p_n-\bar z)$, whose compensator energy is finite. The isometry gives $ \mathbb E\left[ \left\{\frac1{\sqrt n}\int_0^\tau w_n(p_n-\bar z)\,dM_n\right\}^2 \right] \le C^2\Lambda(\tau)\, \mathbb E\!\left[\sup_{t\le\tau}|p_n(t)-\bar z(t)|^2\right]\longrightarrow0. $ The last expectation tends to zero because the supremum is bounded by one and converges to zero in probability by [F5]. Replacing $p_n$ by $\bar z$ therefore changes $U_{n,w_n}/\sqrt n$ by $o_P(1)$.

For the remaining weight replacement, put $D_n=\sum_{g,i}\int_0^\tau(w_n-w)(g-\bar z)\,dM_{gi}$. Since $g$ is constant within each group, $ D_n=\int_0^\tau(w_n-w)(1-\bar z)\,dM_{1,n} -\int_0^\tau(w_n-w)\bar z\,dM_{0,n}. $ Each group aggregate has a simple counting process, continuous compensator, and square-integrable martingale because there are no simultaneous event jumps within that group. Applying [F2]-[F4] to each aggregate and using $(a-b)^2\le2a^2+2b^2$ yields $ \mathbb E[(D_n/\sqrt n)^2] \le 2\Lambda(\tau)\, \mathbb E\!\left[\sup_{t\le\tau}|w_n(t)-w(t)|^2\right]\longrightarrow0. $ Boundedness of $w_n$ and $w$ makes the squared supremum bounded, so its convergence in probability implies convergence of its expectation. Combining the risk-fraction replacement in step 2.1 with this weight replacement proves the stated expansion. No martingale process central limit theorem is used.

filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ in the all-pairs convention of
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. A **simple
unit-jump counting process** is an adapted, càdlàg (right-continuous with left
limits), nondecreasing, integer-valued process $N$ with $N_0=0$,

$Y:[0,T]\times\Omega\to\{0,1\}$, and an **intensity density** is a finite,
nonnegative predictable process $\lambda$. Form the Lebesgue integral
$$A_t:=\int_0^tY_s\lambda_s\,ds,\qquad 0\le t\le T.$$

$$\int_0^tG_s\,dA_s:=\int_0^tG_sY_s\lambda_s\,ds,\qquad t\le T.$$

If $Y_n(t_j)=1$, both groups' product is zero and [F1] assigns variance zero. Thus $ \frac{\widehat V_{n,w_n}}n =\frac1n\int_0^\tau w_n(t)^2p_n(t)(1-p_n(t))\,dN_n(t). $

Uniform convergence of $w_n$ to $w$ and of $p_n$ to $\bar z$, together with their uniform bounds, gives $\sup_{t\le\tau}|w_n(t)^2p_n(t)(1-p_n(t))-w(t)^2\bar z(t)(1-\bar z(t))|\to_P0$. Because $N_n(\tau)\le n$, replacing the integrand in step 1.1 by $h(t):=w(t)^2\bar z(t)(1-\bar z(t))$ changes the normalized integral by at most this supremum, hence by $o_P(1)$.

The aggregate process $N_n$ is simple because no two subjects jump simultaneously, and $A_n(\tau)\le n\Lambda(\tau)$. The deterministic $h$ is bounded and predictable, so [F4]-[F6] give $ \mathbb E\left[\left\{\frac1n\int_0^\tau h(t)\,dM_n(t)\right\}^2\right] =\frac1{n^2}\mathbb E\int_0^\tau h(t)^2\,dA_n(t) \le\frac{\|h\|_\infty^2\Lambda(\tau)}n\longrightarrow0. $ Hence the martingale part of the normalized variance sum tends to zero in probability.

The compensator part of that sum is $ \frac1n\int_0^\tau h(t)\,dA_n(t) =\int_0^\tau h(t)\frac{Y_n(t)}n\lambda(t)\,dt. $ Uniform convergence of $Y_n/n$ to $y$ and $\int_0^\tau\lambda(t)\,dt<\infty$ make this converge in probability to $\int_0^\tau h(t)y(t)\lambda(t)\,dt$. Since $\bar z=y_1/y$, the limit is $\int_0^\tau w(t)^2y_0(t)y_1(t)y(t)^{-1}\lambda(t)\,dt=\sigma_w^2$. Combining this with steps 2.1 and 3.1 proves the assertion.

$\inf_{0\le t\le\tau}y(t)>0$. Set $\bar z(t)=y_1(t)/y(t)$. Let $w_n$ be a common predictable
weight process with $|w_n(t)|\le C$ and a measurable supremum satisfying
$\sup_{t\le\tau}|w_n(t)-w(t)|\to_P0$ for a deterministic bounded predictable
weight $w$. Then the weighted logrank score satisfies
$$\frac{U_{n,w_n}}{\sqrt n} =\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{g=0}^1\sum_{i=1}^{n_g} \int_0^\tau w(t)\bigl(g-\bar z(t)\bigr)\,dM_{gi}(t)+o_P(1).$$
In particular, fixed deterministic bounded predictable weights are included
by taking $w_n=w$.

Assume the two-group common-hazard model with finite-horizon predictable
risk processes and the explicit square-integrable martingale contracts
$M_{gi}=N_{gi}-A_{gi}$, $A_{gi}(t)=\int_0^tY_{gi}(s)\lambda(s)\,ds$; assume
no simultaneous event jumps. Let $Y_{g,n}=\sum_iY_{gi}$,
$Y_n=Y_{0,n}+Y_{1,n}$, and assume the uniform risk-fraction convergence
$Y_n/n\to y$ and $p_n=Y_{1,n}/Y_n\to\bar z$ in probability on $[0,\tau]$,
with $p_n=0$ on an empty risk set (as proved in
[[lem-logrank-risk-fraction-converges]]). Let $w_n\to w$ uniformly in
probability, where the predictable weights are uniformly bounded and $w$
is deterministic. Suppose event times are continuous, so every observed
failure time has $d_j=1$ almost surely. Here $\widehat V_{n,w_n}$ is the
plug-in statistic defined in [[def-logrank-risk-set-score-and-test]]; the
claim is its asymptotic consistency and does not assert an exact finite-sample
conditional variance law. Here $y_0,y_1$ are deterministic nonnegative Borel functions,
$y=y_0+y_1$, $\inf_{0\le t\le\tau}y(t)>0$, and $\bar z=y_1/y$. Define
$$\sigma_w^2:=\int_0^\tau w(t)^2\frac{y_0(t)y_1(t)}{y(t)}\lambda(t)\,dt.$$
Then the weighted plug-in variance sum from
[[def-logrank-risk-set-score-and-test]] satisfies
$$\frac{\widehat V_{n,w_n}}n\longrightarrow_P\sigma_w^2.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix a finite $G\ge2$ and $d\ge1$. For each total sample size $n$, let $n_1,\ldots,n_G$ be positive deterministic integers with $\sum_{g=1}^G n_g=n$, and suppose $n_g/n\to\rho_g\in(0,1)$ with $\sum_{g=1}^G\rho_g=1$. For group $g$, let $O_{g1},O_{g2},\ldots$ be IID with law $P_g$ on a measurable space; assume the subject families in distinct groups are independent. Let $\phi_g$ be measurable with $E_{P_g}\phi_g=0$, $E_{P_g}\|\phi_g\|_2^2<\infty$, and $\Sigma_g=E_{P_g}[\phi_g\phi_g^T]$. If a measurable estimator of fixed $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$ has the separately established expansion, with remainder on the same sample probability space as its group sums,

$$\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta)=\sum_{g=1}^G\sqrt{\frac n{n_g}}\frac1{\sqrt{n_g}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_g}\phi_g(O_{gi})+R_n,\qquad R_n=o_P(1),$$

then

$$\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta)\Rightarrow N_d\!\left(0,\sum_{g=1}^G\rho_g^{-1}\Sigma_g\right).$$

The group count $G$ is fixed; the laws $P_g$ may differ. The covariance may be singular. This is a terminal finite-dimensional result: it neither proves the estimator expansion nor supplies a continuous-time or functional martingale CLT.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Fix a finite horizon
$T>0$, a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ and a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ in the all-pairs convention of
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. A **simple
unit-jump counting process** is an adapted, càdlàg (right-continuous with left
limits), nondecreasing, integer-valued process $N$ with $N_0=0$,
$N_T<\infty$ almost surely, and $\Delta N_t\in\{0,1\}$ for every
$0<t\le T$ outside one null event; here $\Delta N_t:=N_t-N_{t-}$.

An **at-risk process** is a predictable process
$Y:[0,T]\times\Omega\to\{0,1\}$, and an **intensity density** is a finite,
nonnegative predictable process $\lambda$. Form the Lebesgue integral
$$A_t:=\int_0^tY_s\lambda_s\,ds,\qquad 0\le t\le T.$$
For this model and every nonnegative predictable process $G$, define the
pathwise energy integral by
$$\int_0^tG_s\,dA_s:=\int_0^tG_sY_s\lambda_s\,ds,\qquad t\le T.$$
The **continuous intensity compensator contract** requires the defining
integral for $A$ to be finite pathwise, and requires $A$ to be continuous,
adapted and predictable with
$A_0=0$, and that $\mathbb E[A_T]<\infty$. Set $M_t:=N_t-A_t$. The model
contract is the additional hypothesis that $M$ is a square-integrable
martingale relative to the stated filtration. Under this contract $A$ is a
continuous predictable compensator of $N$.

The displayed intensity density alone does **not** assert that $N-A$ is a
martingale, that such a process exists for a given $N$, or that the contract
follows from an empirical observation scheme. No general compensator-existence
theorem is included here. The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the
continuous-time martingale and conditional-expectation interfaces; no further
choice is used to state the model contract.

For the compensator contract on $[0,T]$, let $H$ be a predictable real
process with
$$\mathbb E\int_0^T H_s^2\,dA_s<\infty.$$
When the elementary integrals of a sequence of bounded predictable step
processes converging to $H$ in this norm converge in $L^2(P)$, denote the
resulting $L^2(P)$ class at time $t$ by
$$\int_0^t H_s\,dM_s.$$
The definition is conditional on existence of the limit. The L²-extension
theorem below proves existence for every such predictable $H$, independence
from the approximating sequence, the martingale property, and the isometry.
The Axiom of Choice is inherited through the conditional-expectation and
$L^2$-completion interfaces used by that theorem.

For every predictable $H$ on $[0,T]$ with
$\mathbb E\int_0^T H_s^2\,dA_s<\infty$, the limit in
[[def-l2-counting-process-integral]] exists at each $t\le T$, is independent
of the approximating step sequence, and defines a square-integrable
martingale. It satisfies, for each $t\le T$,
$$\mathbb E\left(\int_0^tH_s\,dM_s\right)^2=\mathbb E\int_0^tH_s^2\,dA_s.$$

Let $X=(X_1,\ldots,X_p)$ be a measurable random vector in $\mathbb R^p$,
where $p\ge1$ is finite, and assume $\mathbb E\|X\|_2^2<\infty$. Define
the mean coordinatewise by $\mu_j=\mathbb E X_j$ and define the covariance
matrix by
$$\Sigma:=\mathbb E[(X-\mu)(X-\mu)^T],$$
where each entry is the expectation of the corresponding real random
variable. Write $\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)=\sum_{j=1}^p\Sigma_{jj}$.

The well-definedness lemma proves these expectations are finite,
$\Sigma$ is symmetric positive semidefinite, and
$\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)=\mathbb E\|X-\mu\|_2^2$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

For a finite family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ of square-integrable real random variables on one common probability space,
$$\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\sum_{i\in I}X_i\right)=\sum_{i\in I}\operatorname{Var}(X_i)+2\sum_{\{i,j\}\subseteq I}\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j).$$
Equivalently, it is $\sum_{i,j\in I}\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j)$. The empty sum has variance zero, and the singleton formula is the identity.
The original finite-probability-space case is included, since every real random variable there is square-integrable and the covariance/variance definitions agree with the finite centered-product/square formulas.
In the first display, the second sum is over two-element subsets of $I$.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

For each positive integer $n$, let $(\Omega_n,\mathcal A_n,P_n)$ be a probability space and let $X_n:\Omega_n\to\mathbb R^d$ be measurable into the Borel sigma-algebra generated by the Euclidean open sets, where $d\ge1$ is fixed and $\mathbb R^d$ has the Euclidean norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]], [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-probability-measure]]). The spaces and measures may depend on $n$; no common probability space is required.

Write $X_n=o_P(1)$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$P_n(\|X_n\|_2>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0.$$
Write $X_n=O_P(1)$, or say that $(X_n)$ is bounded in probability, if for every $\eta>0$ there is $M>0$ such that
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}P_n(\|X_n\|_2>M)\le\eta.$$
For real-valued variables on one common probability space, $o_P(1)$ is convergence in probability to zero as defined in [[def-convergence-in-probability]].

The norms and tail probabilities are part of the definition. Independence is not implicit in either notation.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Let $d,k,m\ge1$ be fixed. For each $n$, let $X_n\in\mathbb R^d$ and $Y_n\in\mathbb R^k$ be random vectors on one probability space; the probability space may vary with $n$. Let $X\in\mathbb R^d$ be a random vector on any probability space, and let $c\in\mathbb R^k$ be constant. If $X_n\Rightarrow X$ and $Y_n-c=o_P(1)$, then
$$ (X_n,Y_n)\Rightarrow(X,c). $$
Consequently, for every continuous $h:\mathbb R^{d+k}\to\mathbb R^m$, $h(X_n,Y_n)\Rightarrow h(X,c)$. No independence between $X_n$ and $Y_n$ is required.

derivations.claim: Put $h_g(t)=w(t)(g-\bar z(t))$. For a subject record $(u,\delta)$, define the real map $ \phi_g(u,\delta)=1\{\delta=1,\ u\le\tau\}h_g(u) -\int_0^{u\wedge\tau}h_g(t)\lambda(t)\,dt. $ The deterministic integrand is bounded and Borel, so its indefinite integral is Borel and this map is measurable. From the definitions of $N_{gi}$, $Y_{gi}$ and $A_{gi}$, this is exactly $\int_0^\tau h_g(t)\,dM_{gi}(t)$. Its energy is at most $\|h_g\|_\infty^2\Lambda(\tau)$; [F8] and [F9] therefore make it square-integrable and centered. It is the same measurable function of each subject record within group $g$, so [F1] makes the transformed records IID within group and [F2] makes the two groups independent.

By [F9] and [F11], $ \mathbb E[\phi_g^2] =\int_0^\tau w(t)^2(g-\bar z(t))^2P(U_{g1}\ge t)\lambda(t)\,dt. $ Multiplying by $\rho_g$ and summing over $g=0,1$ gives $ \sum_{g=0}^1\rho_g\mathbb E[\phi_g^2] =\int_0^\tau w(t)^2\{y_1(t)(1-\bar z(t))^2+y_0(t)\bar z(t)^2\}\lambda(t)\,dt =\sigma_w^2, $ where the last equality follows by substituting $\bar z=y_1/(y_0+y_1)$. The integral is finite since $w$ is bounded, $0\le y_g\le1$, and $\Lambda(\tau)<\infty$.

Fix $\epsilon>0$. Since $n_g\to\infty$, the integrand $\phi_g^2 1\{|\phi_g|>\epsilon\sqrt{n_g}\}$ tends pointwise to zero and is bounded by the integrable $\phi_g^2$. [F15] gives $ n_gP(|\phi_g|>\epsilon\sqrt{n_g}) \le\epsilon^{-2}\mathbb E[\phi_g^2 1\{|\phi_g|>\epsilon\sqrt{n_g}\}] \longrightarrow0. $ Thus each group satisfies the finite-variance no-large-jump condition. Also, for $S_{g,n}=n_g^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^{n_g}\phi_g(U_{gi},\delta_{gi})$, [F1] and [F12] make the cross covariances zero, and [F13] gives $\mathbb E[S_{g,n}^2]=\mathbb E[\phi_g^2]$. Applying [F14] to $S_{g,n}^2$ yields $P(|S_{g,n}|>M)\le\mathbb E[\phi_g^2]/M^2$; hence $S_{g,n}=O_P(1)$ by [F16].

By [A2], the risk-fraction hypotheses used by [F4] hold. Let $\widehat\theta_n=U_{n,w_n}/n$ and set $\theta=0$. By [F4], $ \sqrt n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta) =n^{-1/2}\sum_{g=0}^1\sum_{i=1}^{n_g}\phi_g(U_{gi},\delta_{gi})+o_P(1). $ Set $\psi_g=\rho_g\phi_g$. The group-sum term in [F6] is $ S_n^*=\sum_{g=0}^1\sqrt{\frac n{n_g}}\, \frac1{\sqrt{n_g}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_g}\psi_g(U_{gi},\delta_{gi}). $ Its difference from $n^{-1/2}\sum_{g,i}\phi_g(U_{gi},\delta_{gi})$ equals $ \sum_{g=0}^1\sqrt{\frac n{n_g}}\left(\rho_g-\frac{n_g}n\right)S_{g,n}=o_P(1), $ because $S_{g,n}=O_P(1)$ by step 2.2, $n_g/n\to\rho_g>0$, and there are only two groups. Thus the expansion required by [F6] is established with centered group influences $\psi_g$.

Each $\psi_g$ is centered and square-integrable by step 1.1, and $\operatorname{Var}(\psi_g)=\rho_g^2\mathbb E[\phi_g^2]$ by [F10]. The covariance in [F6] is therefore $ \sum_{g=0}^1\rho_g^{-1}\operatorname{Var}(\psi_g) =\sum_{g=0}^1\rho_g\mathbb E[\phi_g^2]=\sigma_w^2 $ by step 2.1. Applying [F6] to the proved expansion in step 3.1 yields $U_{n,w_n}/\sqrt n\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_w^2)$.

Suppose $\sigma_w^2>0$ and put $V_n=\widehat V_{n,w_n}/n$. By [A2] and [F5], $V_n\to_P\sigma_w^2$, so $P(V_n>\sigma_w^2/2)\to1$. The function $(x,v)\mapsto x/\sqrt{\max(v,\sigma_w^2/2)}$ is continuous everywhere. Apply [F18] and this map to the score limit and $V_n$; the result converges to $Z/\sigma_w$ for $Z\sim N(0,\sigma_w^2)$, which has law $N(0,1)$ by [F17]. On $\{V_n>\sigma_w^2/2\}$ this map equals the stated standardized statistic. Since the complement has probability tending to zero, changing the statistic there has no effect on weak convergence, including any fixed finite extension on the zero-denominator event. When $\sigma_w^2=0$, step 4.1 gives the degenerate score law and no standardized conclusion.

citations.quote:
Fix a follow-up horizon $\tau>0$ and a finite set of subjects
$\mathcal I=\{1,\ldots,n\}$. A right-censored record for subject $i$ is a
pair $(U_i,\delta_i)\in[0,\tau]\times\{0,1\}$, where
$U_i=\min(T_i,C_i)$ is the observed time and
$\delta_i=1\{T_i\le C_i\}$ records an event, including an event-censoring tie;
$\delta_i=0$ records right censoring. A two-group assignment is a map
$z:\mathcal I\to\{0,1\}$. These conventions are the right-censoring
observation scheme; the score below uses the observed record and does not
infer event or censoring laws from it.

Let $t_1<\cdots<t_K$ be the distinct observed failure times in $[0,\tau]$.
For $g\in\{0,1\}$ define the risk count and event count at $t_j$ by
$$Y_{gj}(z):=\#\{i:z_i=g,\ U_i\ge t_j\},\qquad d_{gj}(z):=\#\{i:z_i=g,\ U_i=t_j,\ \delta_i=1\}.$$
Write $Y_j=Y_{0j}+Y_{1j}$, $d_j=d_{0j}+d_{1j}>0$, and
$O_j=d_{1j}$. Since $t_j$ is an observed failure time,
$1\le d_j\le Y_j$. The expected group-1 count under the conditional
hypergeometric model is
$$E_j:=d_j\frac{Y_{1j}}{Y_j}.$$
Under that model the $d_j$ failing subjects are a uniform $d_j$-subset of the
$Y_j$ subjects at risk, conditional on the risk-set and event-count margins.
The corresponding conditional variance is
$$V_j:= \begin{cases} \displaystyle\frac{Y_{1j}Y_{0j}d_j(Y_j-d_j)} {Y_j^2(Y_j-1)},&Y_j>1,\\[6pt] 0,&Y_j=1. \end{cases}$$
If the study has no observed failures, all sums below are empty and equal zero.
The conditional hypergeometric model is an explicit finite risk-set
assumption; equality of survival laws with arbitrary censoring or subject
heterogeneity does not by itself assert this conditional allocation law.
The uniform law on the finite set of $d_j$-subsets is the uniform finite
probability space of [[def-uniform-finite-probability-space]].

A **weight rule** assigns a real value $w_j$ using only the predeclared time
and information available strictly before the failures at $t_j$; deterministic
bounded time weights are a special case. If
$\sup_j|w_j|<\infty$, define the weighted logrank score and its conditional
variance estimate by
$$U_w(z;U,\delta):=\sum_{j=1}^K w_j(O_j-E_j),\qquad \widehat V_w(z;U,\delta):=\sum_{j=1}^K w_j^2V_j.$$
When $\widehat V_w>0$, set
$Z_w:=U_w/\sqrt{\widehat V_w}$. If $\widehat V_w=0$, this standardized
statistic is left undefined; the unstandardized score remains defined. The
normal calibration is only an approximation until the separate terminal
limit hypotheses are verified. It is not the finite-sample Fisher
randomization p-value.

For a fixed observed record, the displayed scores are statistics in the
measurable-map sense of [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]: each risk count is a
finite sum of Borel indicator functions, and every denominator is positive
at an observed event time. A weight rule is fixed before assignments or
outcomes are inspected and is recomputed by the same rule for any candidate
assignment.

The risk-set table concerns one predeclared event type. If simultaneous
records contain distinct event causes that are not exchangeable, form
separate cause-specific counts $O_{jc}$ and $d_{jc}$ using the same
pre-event risk set; use the displayed hypergeometric variance only for a
cause whose failures are conditionally exchangeable. This definition does
not pool different causes or add their variances without a specified
cross-cause covariance model.
The **Kaplan–Meier estimator** is $\widehat S_n(t)=\prod_{\substack{0\le u\le t:\,\Delta N_n(u)>0}}\left(1-\frac{\Delta N_n(u)}{Y_n(u)}\right)$.

derivations.claim: Integrating the hazards gives, for $t\ge1$, $S_1(t)=e^{-(t+1)}$ and $S_0(t)=e^{-(2t-1)}$; for $0\le t\le1$, $S_1(t)=e^{-2t}$ and $S_0(t)=e^{-t}$. On $[0,1]$, $S_1(t)<S_0(t)$ for $t>0$. For $t\ge1$ their ratio is $S_1(t)/S_0(t)=e^{t-2}$, so they meet at $t=2$ and reverse order after it. Each event-time interval $(0,1)$ and $(2,2.5)$ has positive probability, and the specified censor-time values have positive mass. For every subject required to be censored at $c\in\{1.5,2.5\}$, $P(T>c)=S_g(c)>0$ under its group hazard. Mutual independence of all event and censoring times therefore makes the finite intersection defining the sample pattern have positive probability.

At $t_1$, $(Y_{1},Y_{0},d,O)=(4,2,1,1)$, so the score contribution is $1-4/6=1/3$ and the plug-in variance contribution is $4\cdot2/6^2=2/9$. The two censorings at $1.5$ leave one group-1 subject at risk. At $t_2$, $(Y_{1},Y_{0},d,O)=(1,2,1,0)$, so the score contribution is $0-1/3=-1/3$ and the plug-in variance contribution is $1\cdot2/3^2=2/9$. Hence $U=0$ and $\widehat V=4/9>0$, giving standardized score zero. By [F2], $\widehat S_1(t)=1-1/4=3/4$ for $t_1\le t\le2.5$ because the only group-1 failure is at $t_1$; and $\widehat S_0(t)=1$ for $t<t_2$, then $1-1/2=1/2$ for $t_2\le t\le2.5$. The censorings contribute no product factors. Thus the empirical curves reverse order at $t_2$. The cancellation of the score and the crossing population hazards show why this one sample statistic does not establish equality of the survival laws.

Fix a follow-up horizon $\tau>0$ and a finite set of subjects
$\mathcal I=\{1,\ldots,n\}$. A right-censored record for subject $i$ is a
pair $(U_i,\delta_i)\in[0,\tau]\times\{0,1\}$, where
$U_i=\min(T_i,C_i)$ is the observed time and
$\delta_i=1\{T_i\le C_i\}$ records an event, including an event-censoring tie;
$\delta_i=0$ records right censoring. A two-group assignment is a map
$z:\mathcal I\to\{0,1\}$. These conventions are the right-censoring
observation scheme; the score below uses the observed record and does not
infer event or censoring laws from it.

Let $t_1<\cdots<t_K$ be the distinct observed failure times in $[0,\tau]$.
For $g\in\{0,1\}$ define the risk count and event count at $t_j$ by
$$Y_{gj}(z):=\#\{i:z_i=g,\ U_i\ge t_j\},\qquad d_{gj}(z):=\#\{i:z_i=g,\ U_i=t_j,\ \delta_i=1\}.$$
Write $Y_j=Y_{0j}+Y_{1j}$, $d_j=d_{0j}+d_{1j}>0$, and
$O_j=d_{1j}$. Since $t_j$ is an observed failure time,
$1\le d_j\le Y_j$. The expected group-1 count under the conditional
hypergeometric model is
$$E_j:=d_j\frac{Y_{1j}}{Y_j}.$$
Under that model the $d_j$ failing subjects are a uniform $d_j$-subset of the
$Y_j$ subjects at risk, conditional on the risk-set and event-count margins.
The corresponding conditional variance is
$$V_j:= \begin{cases} \displaystyle\frac{Y_{1j}Y_{0j}d_j(Y_j-d_j)} {Y_j^2(Y_j-1)},&Y_j>1,\\[6pt] 0,&Y_j=1. \end{cases}$$
If the study has no observed failures, all sums below are empty and equal zero.
The conditional hypergeometric model is an explicit finite risk-set
assumption; equality of survival laws with arbitrary censoring or subject
heterogeneity does not by itself assert this conditional allocation law.
The uniform law on the finite set of $d_j$-subsets is the uniform finite
probability space of [[def-uniform-finite-probability-space]].

A **weight rule** assigns a real value $w_j$ using only the predeclared time
and information available strictly before the failures at $t_j$; deterministic
bounded time weights are a special case. If
$\sup_j|w_j|<\infty$, define the weighted logrank score and its conditional
variance estimate by
$$U_w(z;U,\delta):=\sum_{j=1}^K w_j(O_j-E_j),\qquad \widehat V_w(z;U,\delta):=\sum_{j=1}^K w_j^2V_j.$$
When $\widehat V_w>0$, set
$Z_w:=U_w/\sqrt{\widehat V_w}$. If $\widehat V_w=0$, this standardized
statistic is left undefined; the unstandardized score remains defined. The
normal calibration is only an approximation until the separate terminal
limit hypotheses are verified. It is not the finite-sample Fisher
randomization p-value.

For a fixed observed record, the displayed scores are statistics in the
measurable-map sense of [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]: each risk count is a
finite sum of Borel indicator functions, and every denominator is positive
at an observed event time. A weight rule is fixed before assignments or
outcomes are inspected and is recomputed by the same rule for any candidate
assignment.

The risk-set table concerns one predeclared event type. If simultaneous
records contain distinct event causes that are not exchangeable, form
separate cause-specific counts $O_{jc}$ and $d_{jc}$ using the same
pre-event risk set; use the displayed hypergeometric variance only for a
cause whose failures are conditionally exchangeable. This definition does
not pool different causes or add their variances without a specified
cross-cause covariance model.

Fix a finite randomized treatment-assignment model with allowed assignments
$\mathcal Z$ and known law $p$, with unit set $\mathcal I$ as in
[[def-finite-randomized-treatment-assignment-model]]. Fix a map
$\gamma:\mathcal Z\to\{0,1\}^{\mathcal I}$ assigning each allowed assignment
a binary logrank group map. For each subject $i$, let
$(U_i(z),\delta_i(z))\in[0,\tau]\times\{0,1\}$ be the full right-censored
record under assignment $z$. Assume the **record sharp null**: for every $i$,
the pair $(U_i(z),\delta_i(z))$ is constant over all $z\in\mathcal Z$. Fix
before observing assignment or records a bounded logrank weight rule and the
two-sided ordering $T(z)=|U_w(\gamma(z);U,\delta)|$.

The inclusive assignment-tail p-value
$$p_{\rm rand}(z):=\sum_{z'\in\mathcal Z}p(z') 1\{|U_w(\gamma(z');U,\delta)|\ge |U_w(\gamma(z);U,\delta)|\}$$
is superuniform under the assignment law, so it is a valid finite-sample
p-value for the record sharp null. If an auxiliary $V$ is independent of
the assignment and uniform on $[0,1]$, replacing the inclusive tail by the
strict-tail mass plus $V$ times the tied-score mass gives an exactly uniform
p-value. The result uses the actual assignment probabilities and asserts no
validity under a weak average-effect null or under an equal-hazard null alone.

Let $N\ge1$, and let $\mathcal I=\{1,\ldots,N\}$ index the fixed
experimental units at the actual treatment-assignment level. Let
$\mathcal Z$ be a nonempty finite set of allowed assignments. If treatment
is assigned to clusters, each cluster is one indexed unit; no separate
probability-sampling unit is present. The index $i$ identifies that unit,
and no visit or repeated-measurement index is modeled here.

A known assignment law is a function $p:\mathcal Z\to[0,1]$ satisfying
$\sum_{z\in\mathcal Z}p(z)=1$, so $(\mathcal Z,p)$ is a finite probability
space ([[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]); assignments of probability
zero may remain in $\mathcal Z$. A **potential-outcome schedule** is a function
$\theta:\mathcal I\times\mathcal Z\to\mathbb R$, with
$Y_i(z):=\theta(i,z)$. The schedule and the units are fixed; the assignment
$Z$ is the only randomness supplied by the design, and the observed response
vector is $Y_\theta(Z)=(Y_i(Z))_{i\in\mathcal I}$. The schedule is defined
for every allowed assignment, including zero-probability assignments, and
may depend on the full assignment vector, so no no-interference assumption is
implicit. The scientific statistical model contract
[[def-scientific-statistical-model-contract]] requires the observation space,
units, quantity status, observation mechanism, support, conditioning
convention, and adequacy assumptions to be recorded; this model specifies
those fields as follows.

To express this as a statistical experiment, take the data space
$\mathcal X=\mathcal Z\times\mathbb R^{\mathcal I}$ with its full power-set
sigma-algebra, which is a sigma-algebra by [[def-sigma-algebra]] and makes
$\mathcal X$ a measurable space ([[def-measurable-space]]), and parameter
set $\Theta=\mathbb R^{\mathcal I\times\mathcal Z}$. For each $\theta\in\Theta$
let $P_\theta$ be the law
([[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]) of the deterministic
observation map $O_\theta(z)=(z,Y_\theta(z))$ from $(\mathcal Z,p)$. The map
is measurable because its domain has the full power set, in the preimage
sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]], and its law
is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]]. Thus
$((\mathcal X,2^{\mathcal X}),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ is an
experiment in the sense of [[def-statistical-experiment]]. The assignment
law asserts no response-error model, Gaussian law, superpopulation
randomization, or sampling representativeness beyond the stated finite
assignment mechanism. Its finite full-measure support set is
$$S_\theta:=\{(z,Y_\theta(z)):z\in\mathcal Z,\ p(z)>0\},$$
since $P_\theta(S_\theta)=\sum_{z:p(z)>0}p(z)=1$. The record contains the
assigned vector and every unit's response; missing or censored outcomes and
repeated visits require a separately declared observation mechanism. The
inferential target is the assignment-invariance hypothesis for these $N$
units, not an estimand for a wider population.

Inference in this page holds $\mathcal I$ and $\theta$ fixed and averages
over the declared law $p$; it does not condition on the realized assignment.
The status of the quantities is explicit: $\theta$ and all
$Y_i(z)$ are fixed, $Z$ is random, $(Z,Y_\theta(Z))$ is observed, and
potential responses under unassigned vectors are fixed but latent. The
assignment set, weights, and implemented randomization protocol are
design-controlled and should be checked against protocol records. Assignment
logs and response records are empirically assessable, but those checks do not
prove that the declared law generated the data. Potential outcomes under
unassigned vectors are fixed and latent in the realized record. This does
not imply nonidentifiability from the observed-data law: for each $z$ with
$p(z)>0$, the law assigns mass $p(z)$ to $(z,Y_\theta(z))$, and therefore
determines $Y_\theta(z)$. Assignment invariance on this positive-probability
set is **empirically assessable**, and the theorem tests the stronger
invariance hypothesis on all allowed assignments. Values at assignments
with $p(z)=0$, and restrictions on those values, are **substantively
untestable** from this law, since changing them leaves $P_\theta$ unchanged.
One realized assignment does not reveal responses at other assignments.
These classifications do not make the design or scientific model
empirically true.

derivations.claim: The prescribed full record for each subject is identical under all three allowed assignments, so the full-record sharp-null hypothesis in [F2] holds. Under the map $\gamma(e_1)$, the event at time 1 contributes $1-1/3=2/3$ and the later risk sets contain no treated subject, so $U(\gamma(e_1))=2/3$. Under $\gamma(e_2)$, time 1 contributes $-1/3$, and time 2 contributes $1-1/2=1/2$, giving $U(\gamma(e_2))=1/6$. Under $\gamma(e_3)$, time 1 contributes $-1/3$, time 2 contributes $-1/2$, and time 3 contributes zero, giving $U(\gamma(e_3))=-5/6$. These are the three distinct scores; their absolute values are $2/3,1/6,5/6$.

The inclusive absolute-tail probability at $e_1$ is $1/2+1/6=2/3$, at $e_2$ it is $1$, and at $e_3$ it is $1/6$, because the absolute scores are distinct and the assignment weights are $1/2,1/3,1/6$. Therefore the p-value takes $2/3,1,1/6$ with respective probabilities $1/2,1/3,1/6$.

Its distribution function is $0$ for $0\le u<1/6$, $1/6$ for $1/6\le u<2/3$, $2/3$ for $2/3\le u<1$, and $1$ at $u=1$. On each interval this is at most $u$, including the endpoints. Thus the exact finite assignment calculation is superuniform under the declared unequal-weight law, as in [F2].
